HCBCOGN312.name: Psycholinguistics
HCBCOGN312.contribution: Direct study of acquisition, bilingualism, comprehension, semantics, production and impairments, with hands-on experiments.
HCBCOGN312.topics: Psycholinguistics is the study of the neurobiological and psychological factors that enable us to acquire, use, and understand language. Modern research draws on cognitive psychology, neuroscience, and computer science to investigate how language is processed. The course focuses primarily, though not exclusively, on the neuroscience of language. Students examine theoretical and experimental issues in speech production and comprehension, language impairments, the relationship between thought and language, and the evolution and acquisition of language. They also gain hands-on experience with experimental approaches to the study of language and develop an understanding of human linguistic capacity as a subject of multidisciplinary research. Topics covered: What is language? Evolutionary aspects of language and animal communication; language and thought; aphasia; language acquisition; bilingualism; speech comprehension; semantics; reading and dyslexia; speech production.

findings: The first plan combines language processing, style and meaning, experiments, cognition, discourse and qualitative research. Psycholinguistics is directly relevant and Style & Meaning teaches linguistic analysis of grammar and pragmatics in texts. Ethnography, interviewing and research design supply transferable inquiry methods, without elicitation and documentation of unfamiliar language structures.

The second plan adds programming, strings, algorithms, text data, applied learning and transformer models. Text classification and generation are concrete content. It provides computational language tools with a smaller discourse and cognition core, without reproducing a sequence in linguistic typology or field documentation.

The current workbook was searched for phonetics, phonology, morphology, syntax, semantics, sociolinguistics, language history, acquisition, neurolinguistics, field elicitation, typology and language data. Everyday Dutch, stylistics and qualitative methods provide bounded overlap but no comparative historical or descriptive fieldwork progression. Full programme comparability remains provisional until the source gap is resolved.
